caveats: **The fast open is more permissive than the walk in two ancestor-only cases.** An ancestor the caller may traverse but not read: the walk answers `access_denied`, the fast open accepts. An ordinary non-link ancestor that carries a value named `SymbolicLinkValue`: the link probe cannot tell it from a link, so the walk answers `key_is_link` and the fast open accepts. In both the write lands on the real requested key, which is what registry 1.0.0's single open did; probing every ancestor on the fast path would cost it the constant call count. A decoy value on the LEAF of a `set_value` or `delete_value` is refused on both paths (a `delete_key` leaf is opened as a possible link, so it is not probed). `HKCU`, `HKCR`, a missing key and any failed name query take the walk (same verdicts, more calls; a name query that keeps failing refuses there too). A path whose case differs from the stored spelling only outside ASCII declines the fast open, and the walk then refuses it `key_is_link` (every component, the first included, is compared with the kernel's name by the same ASCII-only fold): write such a key with its stored spelling. If the kernel name of `HKLM` or `HKU` cannot be read at the first write, the fast open is off for that root until the agent restarts. **`HKCR` may be refused `key_is_link` where its merged view reaches the other backing hive.** `HKCR` merges `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes` with the calling user's classes hive (the agent runs as `SYSTEM`, so that half is `HKU\.DEFAULT_Classes`). The walk requires the leaf's kernel name to equal the first component's name plus the rest of the requested path, the same compare for every hive; if the merged view resolves a lower component into the other backing hive than the first component, the two names differ and the write is refused `key_is_link` with nothing written, although no link is involved. A refusal is the failure mode, never an unverified write. Measured on Windows 11 (2026-10-23): for an interactive user a key whose first component exists in both backing hives and whose lower component exists only in the machine hive IS refused `key_is_link` (the first component is bound to the user hive, the lower one to `HKLM`); the reverse orientation and every key wholly inside one hive are accepted. As `SYSTEM`, the agent's identity, `HKCR` shows only `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes`, so the shape does not arise there. If an `HKCR` write is refused, write under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes` or `HKU\<SID>_Classes` directly. **`HKCU\Software\Classes` is a registry link for a real user.** Measured on Windows (2026-10-25): For a real user's hive `HKCU\Software\Classes` is itself a registry link (to the user's `_Classes` hive), so a creating write below it is refused `key_is_link` (1.0.0 followed it); as SYSTEM, the agent's identity, `HKCU` is `HKU\.DEFAULT` and `Software\Classes` is not a link, so such writes succeed; to write a user's classes use `hive=HKU` with `<SID>_Classes`.

**The audit trail is lossy by design.** Key and value names go through `audit_token`, which applies `yuzu::log_token` (space, `=`, `,`, control bytes, DEL, `|` become `_`, and so does a trailing backslash) and then `fold_line_breaks` (the C1 controls U+0080-U+009F and U+2028 and U+2029 become `_`; over 256 bytes, measured after folding, they are cut with `~<length>`), and old/new data is hex capped at 256 raw bytes, so an audit row identifies the change but cannot always reproduce it (a value cut at 256 bytes cannot be rebuilt from it, and the hex can hold a secret: owner risk acceptance, see "Sensitivity"); a `delete_key` row carries counts, not values: `old=-|new=-`; `old=` and the delete counts are point in time; the single actions accept a value named `-`, whose audit line renders `name=-` exactly like the default value. Rows exist only for agents that stamp `CommandResponse.action`: an agent at v0.14.1 or earlier writes registry values but produces no `registry.write` rows, and a read action never does. **An exception inside a mutating action** (an allocation failure while capturing, writing or reading back is the realistic one) is contained at the plugin ABI seam: the plugin writes a fixed failed audit line (`result=failed`, `reason=exception`, every other field `-`, so `created=-` and no `old=`/`new=`) and then `error|exception` with rc 1, and the server records that line as a failed `registry.write` row. For `apply` the fixed line is `op=apply` and follows the rows of the items already done (items 0 to N-1 when item N threw). A creating write tries to remove the keys it made, and the value it had written into them, on an exception before its verified write ends (best effort, below); a write onto an existing key that had already landed keeps its value, and so does a write whose exception came after its verified write (while the reply was being built): the row says `failed`, and the key must be read back to know. An agent that dies mid-command loses every row it had not yet sent (it sends at command end or each 64 KiB), so a single action, or a small `apply`, leaves no row at all; the server's `command.dispatch` row and the stored response keep the attempt attributable. The rollback is BEST EFFORT: a key that holds a value or a subkey when it checks is kept and, on a returning exit, counted in `created=` (`result=failed`), and `created=` can also count a key another party deleted first, which the rollback then cannot delete again. A write that lands between the check and the delete, or over our own same-named value before the rollback deletes it by name, can still be lost, because Windows has no delete-if-empty call. After a double fault (a rollback step that fails or throws) the value and the keys may stay with `created=-` and nothing logged. "Where the data goes" has the procedure for what a failed create can leave.

**Behaviour changes from 1.0.** The changes to existing actions are listed in the 2.0.0 changelog entry (`changelog.d/2026-10-22-registry-typed-writes.changed.md`) and in `docs/user-manual/upgrading.md`, which also gives the rollout order (server replicas first) and the minimum agent version for `registry.write` rows (the first release that contains the audit binding of #6294, later than 0.14.1). **Mixed fleets:** an agent still running registry 1.x writes an EMPTY `REG_SZ` over the value for a `data_hex`-only `set_value` (it reads only `name`, `value` and `type`; with `type=REG_DWORD` and `data_hex` only it throws and writes nothing), stores `REG_QWORD`, `REG_MULTI_SZ`, `REG_EXPAND_SZ` and `REG_BINARY` values as `REG_SZ` text, reports `status|ok` for all of those, and follows a write under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet` that 2.0.0 refuses; nothing on the server gates dispatch on a plugin version (the definitions' `minAgentVersion` is declared and exported, not compared at dispatch), so upgrade the agents before using the new types or `data_hex`, in schedules, workflows, policies and bundles as well as scripts. **Embedded NUL:** a NUL inside a parameter sent through `POST /api/command` reaches the plugin as a C string and cuts the value at the NUL on every agent version (the instruction and MCP routes refuse control bytes), so a key or value name that carries one writes a shorter key or name than the one sent. A reply that is a bare `status|ok` with no leading `audit|` row came from a 1.x agent: read the value back with `get_value`. **An existing server install keeps the 1.0.0 definitions:** bundled definitions are inserted only when absent, so an install that already holds `windows.registry.set_value`, `delete_value` and `delete_key` keeps their 1.0.0 text, enum and parameters (no `data_hex`, a `type` enum of `REG_SZ` and `REG_DWORD` only, `value` required) until they are replaced, and a stored `windows.registry.get_value` keeps its 1.0.0 description (only its text changed in 1.1.0): export, delete and re-import the four definitions, `get_value` included (`docs/user-manual/instructions.md`, "Replacing a stored parameter schema") to get the 1.1.0 text, enum and `data_hex`. Until the fleet is upgraded, scope such a write to upgraded devices (`ostype == "windows" AND tag:<key> == "<value>"`, with a tag that marks the upgraded devices) or switch the action off with the `set_value` kill switch. **2.0.0 asks the key for more access than 1.0.0 did.** `set_value` opens the leaf with `KEY_SET_VALUE` and `KEY_QUERY_VALUE` (the read-back and the link probe need the second), and `KEY_CREATE_SUB_KEY` on each parent it creates under; `delete_value` the same two on the leaf; `delete_key` `DELETE`, `KEY_ENUMERATE_SUB_KEYS` and `KEY_QUERY_VALUE`; the walk adds `KEY_QUERY_VALUE` on every component it passes through. An ACL that grants less answers `access_denied`. **Creating a key now asks for `DELETE` on it**, so that a walk that stops can remove what it made by handle: where an inherited ACL gives the agent identity no `DELETE` on a new key (SYSTEM and Administrators have it on the usual parents) the create answers `access_denied`, and there is deliberately no retry without it. **2.1.0 mixed fleets: a registry 1.x or 2.0.x agent (every agent released before 2.1.0, v0.14.1 included) sent `dry_run=true` DELETES a leaf key.** `do_delete_key` there reads neither `recursive` nor `dry_run`: a `delete_key` with `dry_run=true` on a key with no subkeys deletes it (a key with subkeys is refused), and `recursive=true` is ignored the same way; a bare `status|ok` (1.x) or a `dry_run|0` row (2.0.x) in answer to `dry_run=true` means the key WAS deleted. `set_user_value`, `delete_user_value` and `apply` answer `error|unknown action` there. Nothing on the server compares a plugin version at dispatch (the definitions' `minAgentVersion` is declared and exported, not compared; the root-cause tracker is #6484), so upgrade the server, then the agents to registry 2.1.0, and scope any preview to a tag that marks devices verified at 2.1.0, in schedules, workflows, policies and bundles as well as scripts; until then the `delete_key` kill switch (`?action=delete_key`) is the stop-gap. As declared, the `minAgentVersion: 0.15.0` pin (on `delete_key` 1.2.0, the three new definitions and `set_value`) separates registry 1.x (v0.14.1) from 2.1.0 but cannot separate 2.0.x from 2.1.0 if both first ship in 0.15.0. `delete_key` definition 1.2.0 needs a re-import on an existing server install (bundled definitions are inserted only when absent); re-import it only after every targeted agent is verified at 2.1.0, because the stored definition without `dry_run` is what keeps the instruction route from sending it (`docs/user-manual/upgrading.md`).

**`delete_key` without `recursive` removes only a key with no subkeys; the per-user writes and `apply` have limits of their own.** A key with subkeys is refused `key_has_subkeys` and nothing is deleted. The key's own values go with it, and the counts are a point-in-time read of them. A subkey created between the check and the delete cannot be refused as `key_has_subkeys`: `NtDeleteKey` refuses the delete and the action answers a failure token (`access_denied` or `win32:<code>`, not `key_has_subkeys`), with the key still in place and nothing deleted. `recursive=true` has its own bound and its own races ("How it works"): a tree over 10,000 keys and values or 600 levels cannot be deleted in one call (`tree_too_large`); the counts of a dry run are a snapshot and the counts of the real run are what it removed, which can be more; a registry link anywhere in the tree refuses the whole call. **Per-user writes: what the offline arm cannot promise.** The offline mount is serialised process-wide under the offline-hive lock (a long write holds it, and with it every other offline hive reader); the write is bounded by 1 MiB plus one flush. The post-unload probe sees a hive loaded AFTER the write returned; a logon that failed while the hive was mounted leaves no trace, and the probe cannot tell a hive loaded by another actor from a failed one. A flush that fails fails the write although the verified value is in the mounted hive (durability unknown); a creating write's keys are rolled back, an overwrite keeps its value. A mount that is refused or fails to load writes nothing. A mount that fails to unload after a durable write (`hive_unload_failed`) stays until `reg unload` or a reboot, and so does one left by an agent that died mid-write: the user's next logon can get a temporary profile and the next offline write for that profile answers `hive_mount_failed`; the plugin neither retries the unload nor sweeps old mounts (#5292, #3140). The privileges are enabled on the process token for the span of the mount (`with_user_hive`). **`apply` limits.** Machine hive only (`HKLM`): a per-user bulk apply is not built. Not transactional, with an undo you read from the reply, not a rollback; the manifest is bounded (one 512 KiB budget; an incomplete one says `undo_complete|0`, in the dry run too). A dry run cannot see the ACL a key that does not exist yet will inherit ("How it works"), so `would_apply` is a prediction for a missing key and a fact for an existing one; the create probe is measured only on Windows (`tests/unit/test_registry_win_internals.cpp`). Keys that differ only in non-ASCII case are not recognised as one key by `dependent_items` or by the per-key handle map, so such a plan opens the key twice (the kernel folds them; the plugin's ASCII-only fold is a strict subset). Value names are handled conservatively instead: two value items on one key are `dependent_items` whenever either name holds a non-ASCII character. The vet bound is per item: each `delete_key` item can vet up to 10,000 values, so a plan of 256 large leaves vets millions with no deadline. The value-op items on one key share a handle opened with `KEY_QUERY_VALUE` and `KEY_SET_VALUE`; a key op is always alone on its key. A value named `-`, a name ending in a backslash and any name the row spelling cannot carry are refused ("The exact-name rule"); the default value (empty name) is spelt `-` in a row. A dry run mints `registry.write` rows (`result=success`, `dry_run=1`), and a 256-item plan is up to 256 of the 600 rows an agent may write per minute.

**Three read-side gaps are unchanged.** `get_value` is bounded at 1 MiB since 2.0.1. `enumerate_values` writes `value|<name>|<type>` (the leading `value` is a literal tag, not a third column), `get_value`/`enumerate_values` leave `REG_MULTI_SZ`/`REG_LINK` values hex-encoded where `get_user_value` decodes them (changing that changes `get_value`'s output for existing callers), and `PrivilegeScope`'s `AdjustTokenPrivileges` call must keep its `ReturnLength` argument (without it the offline fallback silently never enabled the privileges until #2771: `agents/shared/win_profiles.hpp`, `changelog.d/2771-privilegescope-token-adjust-bug.fixed.md`). The `get_user_value` capture exercised the live-hive path, not the offline mount. `get_value` reads at most 1 MiB (2.0.1), the bound `get_user_value` and the write path already use: a larger value answers `error|value exceeds 1 MiB limit` with rc 1, so a value that any writer of the key made huge is never read whole into the agent's memory (three copies: the bytes, their hex and the sanitised string). Registry 2.0.0 and earlier read the whole value. **Read output is display text.** In every registry-controlled string the read actions render (names, subkey names, decoded string data), `|`, the control characters except TAB, DEL, the C1 controls, U+2028 and U+2029 each become `_` and trailing NULs are dropped, so the exact characters cannot be recovered from a row: `a<U+2028>b`, `a<VT>b` and `a_b` render alike. `get_value` has no exact-bytes mode for a string value (the types it returns as hex are exact); before 2.0.1 an embedded NUL in a name or in `get_value` data cut the row short instead; `get_user_value` reads a string value up to its first NUL. A name that ends in a NUL renders the same as the name without it.

definitions.description: Apply a declarative plan of machine-hive (HKLM) changes -- set_value, delete_value, create_key and non-recursive delete_key items -- with a dry run, read-back verification of value writes and deletes (a created key is evidenced by its create disposition, an existing one by being opened) and an undo manifest in the response; nothing is persisted on the endpoint. Dry run is the default: pass dry_run=false to change anything. Each key is opened ONCE on a checked handle (a registry symbolic link is refused, never followed) and every item on it reuses that handle; the previous value is captured before it is changed, and an item whose previous value this plugin could not write back (a type it cannot write, a shape it would refuse) is refused before anything changes. A dry run and a real run take ONE verdict function over the same facts, so they agree item for item (would_apply or applied, or refused); a plan is refused whole as dependent_items when two items touch the same value or a key item overlaps another item's key. The dry run opens with the mutation's own access mask and checks create access on the deepest existing key, but it cannot see the ACL a key that does not exist yet will inherit: a real run can still be refused or fail where the dry run said would_apply (the keys it made are rolled back by handle and `created` reports any that stayed). NOT transactional: with continue_on_error=false the first refused or failed item stops the run and the rest are skipped; the exit code is non-zero whenever any item was refused or failed. THE EXACT-NAME RULE: every key path and value name the manifest carries must read back as exactly what is in the registry, so a name that a row cannot spell (a `|`, a control character, a C1 control, U+2028 or U+2029, invalid UTF-8, a trailing backslash, or a value named `-`, which a row uses for the default value) is refused as unrepresentable_name before anything is changed, including the name of any value of a key an item would delete, whose raw UTF-16 name must also be well-formed (a lone surrogate or a NUL has no exact UTF-8 spelling and is refused the same way, in a dry run too; a value really named with U+FFFD is fine). Two value items on one key are also dependent_items whenever either name holds a non-ASCII character (Windows folds value-name case with a Unicode table the parser cannot reproduce). THE UNDO BUDGET: one 512 KiB budget charges every byte the manifest retains (previous values up to 4,096 bytes each, names and a fixed cost per row); a deleted key's values are all vetted but only as many as fit are returned, and when anything was cut the summary says undo_complete=0, in the dry run too, before anything is changed. THE UNDO CONTRACT: undo only `applied` items and `failed` ones with created above 0 or a mutation, in REVERSE item order; recreate a deleted key from its delete_key item (a key that held no values has no undo rows), then replay its undo rows in a second plan (a value whose name holds a non-ASCII character in a plan of its own when the key has other undo rows). The manifest restores VALUES only: a deleted key's owner, DACL, SACL, class and volatility are not captured, so a recreated key gets the parent's inherited security. It is a snapshot taken at capture: a value another writer changes between the capture and the change is lost or stale even with undo_complete=1. An item refused before its previous value was read shows "-" there, never "absent". Rows are written as each item concludes, so a later exception inside the plugin or a failed output channel cannot take back rows already written; the agent sends output at command end or each 64 KiB, so an agent that dies mid-plan loses whatever it had not sent (for a plan whose output is under 64 KiB, all of it): read the keys back with a dry run before replaying anything. The rows: one `audit` row per item that ran or was refused (recorded server-side as `registry.write`; a dry run's rows say dry_run=1 and record no change; three 256-item plans inside one minute exceed the server's 600 rows per agent per minute and the later rows are suppressed), its `item` row and, for a deleted key, its `undo` rows, then a closing `summary`. The plan parameter, with every value in it, is stored unredacted in the execution's parameter_values, and the reply holds previous values (secrets included) for Response:Read holders. Needs registry 2.1.0 on the agent: an agent at registry 1.x or 2.0.x answers `error|unknown action`. Windows-only.

Delete a Windows registry key. By default only a key with no subkeys is deleted (one with subkeys is refused as key_has_subkeys and nothing is deleted); `recursive` true removes the key and everything beneath it, and `dry_run` true counts what a real run would remove and deletes nothing. The key is opened on a checked handle (one canonical-name-checked open, with a component walk as the fallback) and a registry symbolic link in the path is refused, never followed (the key AT the path may itself be a link: the link object is removed and its target is untouched). A recursive delete first VETS the whole tree: every child is opened from its parent's handle with the delete's own access and probed for a link, and a link anywhere in the tree is refused as key_is_link with nothing deleted (a child whose ACL denies the delete, as access_denied, in a dry run too; a key whose raw UTF-16 name is not well-formed, which no UTF-8 name can open exactly, as unrepresentable_name). It then removes the tree post-order, each key by its own handle (no RegDeleteTreeW, which follows links), re-checking every key it finds for a link: a link planted since the vet stops the delete as key_is_link, and a tree that grew past the vet's bound stops it as concurrent_change, with what was already removed counted. The vet is a size bound and a link sweep, not a list of the keys it saw: a key added after it is deleted and counted like any other. It visits at most 10,000 keys and values and 600 levels; a dry run past that reports a lower bound with capped=1, and a real recursive delete of a tree it could not finish is refused as tree_too_large with nothing deleted (delete it in parts). On a dry run or a refusal the counts are what the vet counted; on a real run they are what the delete removed (exact when it succeeds, the partial total when it stopped), so they can exceed a dry run's. A non-recursive delete of a key holding more than 10,000 values removes only that key and its own values. MIXED FLEETS: an agent running registry 1.x or 2.0.x (every agent released before 2.1.0, v0.14.1 included) reads neither `recursive` nor `dry_run`: sent dry_run=true it DELETES a key that has no subkeys (a key with subkeys is refused), and a bare `status|ok` or a `dry_run|0` row in answer to dry_run=true means the key was deleted. The server does not compare plugin versions at dispatch (#6484), so upgrade the server, then the agents to registry 2.1.0 before using either flag, scope any preview to a tag that marks devices verified at 2.1.0, and until then use the delete_key kill switch as the stop-gap. Windows-only.

Delete a registry value from a specific user's hive; the key itself is left in place. Same profile resolution, live-or-offline hive path, hive-file guard, read-back verification, flush and audit row as set_user_value (the deleted value's previous data is in that row and in the response). Needs registry 2.1.0 on the agent: an agent at registry 1.x or 2.0.x answers `error|unknown action`. Windows-only.

Delete a specific value from a Windows registry key; the key itself is left in place. Registry 2.0.0 reports a failure as an `error|<token>` line (key_not_found, value_not_found, key_is_link, access_denied ...) instead of a sentence, limits the key path to 255 bytes and 32 components, and emits one leading `audit|op=delete_value|...` row (the old value, hex) before `status|ok`. Windows-only.
List all immediate subkeys under a registry key, one row per subkey. Windows-only.
List all value names and types under a Windows registry key, one row per value. Value data itself is not returned — use get_value to read a specific value. Windows-only.

Read a registry value from a specific user's registry hive. Resolves the target profile via ProfileList (by username or an explicit SID), then reads the live HKEY_USERS\<SID> hive if the user is logged in, or loads that profile's NTUSER.DAT via RegLoadKey as a fallback. SeBackupPrivilege and SeRestorePrivilege are required only for the offline fallback when the target user is not logged in; reading an already-loaded live hive needs no elevated privilege. Windows-only.

Read a value from the Windows registry. Value data is decoded for REG_SZ/REG_EXPAND_SZ/REG_DWORD/REG_QWORD; every other type, including REG_MULTI_SZ and REG_LINK, is returned as hex-encoded bytes rather than decoded (get_user_value decodes both of those). Windows-only.
Check whether a registry key exists, without reading any of its values. Windows-only.

Enumerate local Windows user profiles from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList: SID, resolved profile name, profile path, and whether the profile's registry hive is currently loaded under HKEY_USERS. System profiles (LocalSystem, LocalService, NetworkService) are excluded. Windows-only.

Write a registry value into a specific user's hive. Resolves the target profile via ProfileList (by username or an explicit SID), then writes through the live HKEY_USERS\<SID> hive if the user is logged in, or loads that profile's NTUSER.DAT as a fallback. The offline load runs behind the shared hive-file guard (reparse ancestors, a second hard link, ownership, transaction-log sidecars and the file identity after the load are checked first), the write is verified by reading it back, and the key is flushed to disk before the hive unloads (a flush that fails fails the write). SeBackupPrivilege and SeRestorePrivilege are needed only for the offline fallback. A hive that is loaded after the write returned is reported as a warning; a logon that failed while the hive was mounted leaves no trace. Same types, encoding and verification as set_value. A `registry.write` audit row records the previous and new values (hex, capped at 256 bytes; they can contain secrets: the product owner accepted this risk on 2026-10-20 and masking is a planned later change), and the `value` and `data_hex` parameters are stored unredacted in the execution's parameter_values. Needs registry 2.1.0 on the agent: an agent at registry 1.x or 2.0.x answers `error|unknown action`. Windows-only.

Write a value to the Windows registry, creating missing key components beneath an existing top-level key (a path whose first component is missing is refused as root_level_create). All six writable types are supported (REG_SZ, REG_EXPAND_SZ, REG_BINARY, REG_DWORD, REG_MULTI_SZ, REG_QWORD) and the write is verified: the previous value is captured first, the new one is read back on the same handle and compared byte for byte, and a mismatch fails the action. The key is opened on a checked handle (one canonical-name-checked open, with a component walk as the fallback) and a registry symbolic link anywhere in the path is refused, never followed; a write under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet, itself a link, therefore fails as key_is_link. The previous and new values are recorded in a `registry.write` audit row (hex, capped at 256 bytes; they can contain secrets: the product owner accepted this risk on 2026-10-20 and masking is a planned later change). Needs registry 2.0.0 on the agent: an agent still running registry 1.x writes an EMPTY REG_SZ for a data_hex-only write, stores REG_QWORD, REG_MULTI_SZ, REG_EXPAND_SZ and REG_BINARY values as REG_SZ text and follows a write under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet, all answering `status|ok`, so upgrade the agents first. Windows-only.

description: Windows Registry -- get, set (six types, verified), delete value, delete key (optionally recursive), enumerate, per-user reads and writes, bulk apply with an undo manifest
how_it_works:
All twelve actions are direct, synchronous Win32 registry calls: there is no scheduled gather. The six read actions (`get_value`, `key_exists`, `enumerate_keys`, `enumerate_values`, `get_user_value`, `list_profiles`) open a key read-only and read or list it; every registry-controlled string they render passes through `sanitize_field` (trailing NULs are dropped; `|`, every control character except TAB (CR, LF, ESC and an interior NUL among them), DEL, the C1 controls U+0080-U+009F and U+2028 and U+2029 each become `_`), so no read output can contain a line that starts with `audit|`, split a log line, start a terminal escape or be cut short at the plugin ABI. `get_user_value` and `list_profiles` read a REG_SZ, REG_EXPAND_SZ or REG_LINK value up to its first NUL, as Windows does, so data after an interior NUL is not shown there; `get_value` shows it as `_`. The rendered text is DISPLAY text: the folded characters cannot be recovered from a row, so two names that differ only in one of them render alike (caveat 5). `get_user_value` resolves the target profile through the same `ProfileList` walk `list_profiles` exposes, reads the live `HKEY_USERS\<SID>` hive if the user is logged in, and falls back to an offline `RegLoadKeyW` mount of `NTUSER.DAT` (under `SeBackup`/`SeRestore` and a process-wide mutex serialising the whole offline arm) only when the user is logged out. The seven `hive`+`key` actions validate through one `parse_target` helper, which also logs (never blocks) access to a few sensitive `HKLM` subtrees via `spdlog::info`.

The six mutating actions (`set_value`, `delete_value`, `delete_key`, `set_user_value`, `delete_user_value`, `apply`) share one core (`registry_core.hpp`, over an injected registry; `registry_win.cpp` binds it to `Reg*W`). Each obtains a CHECKED handle for the key, and every step after that -- the previous-value capture, `RegSetValueExW`, the verifying read-back, `RegDeleteValueW`, `NtDeleteKey(h)` -- runs on that handle: nothing re-resolves the path by name, and no handle outlives the command. There are two ways to the handle.

- **The fast open (`HKLM` and `HKU` only).** ONE `RegOpenKeyExW` of the whole path with `REG_OPTION_OPEN_LINK`, then `NtQueryKey(KeyNameInformation)` names the object the handle is bound to. The open is accepted only when that kernel name equals `<root kernel name>\<requested path>` (every byte exact except that A-Z fold, so a name that differs in non-ASCII case, a name that does not fit the 4 KiB buffer and a failed query all decline) and the leaf has no `SymbolicLinkValue`. A registry link before the leaf makes the kernel open the link's TARGET, whose name cannot equal the requested one, so the fast open can only accept the canonical object with no real link traversed; everything else declines to the walk. A `set_value` on an existing key is 7 calls across the plugin's registry seam (`open_path`, `final_name`, the link probe, capture, set, read-back, close; the cached root-name lookup is an eighth), the same at every depth, and about 7 Win32 calls: the link probe, the capture and the read-back are each one `RegQueryValueExW` for a value that fits a 256-byte first buffer (a larger value costs one more read). The walk costs about 3 more per path component, plus two name queries.
- **The walk (the reference).** `open_checked` walks the path component by component from the hive root, opening each component from the previous HANDLE with `REG_OPTION_OPEN_LINK` and probing it for `SymbolicLinkValue`: a registry link is refused (`key_is_link`), never followed. A probe only sees the key as it is at that instant, and a link is made in two steps (the key, then its `SymbolicLinkValue`), so the walk also ends on the fast open's test. It reads the canonical kernel name of the FIRST component's handle right after that open (before its probe; it has to end in the requested first component, else `key_is_link`) and of the leaf handle at the end (after the create loop too), and hands the leaf over only when the leaf's name equals the first component's name plus the remaining requested components (A-Z fold). A link completed after its probe, or a component moved away by a rename, leaves the handle bound to an object whose name is not the requested path: the action is refused `key_is_link` and no value is written, and a name that cannot be read is refused with its Win32 token (including one holding a NUL or a lone surrogate: `win32:13`). A link completed during the create loop is the one case where the walk has already written: a create is relative to a handle the kernel parses again, so the keys can land beneath the link's target. The keys a creating walk makes stay owned by the operation until its verified write is over (`Opened::made`; its destructor is the rollback). So a walk that does not hand its leaf over (the name test refuses, a later create fails, or a later create finds its key already there), and an exception anywhere from the first create to the end of the verified write (an allocation failure while capturing the previous value, writing or reading back), try to delete every key the walk created, by its own handle, leaf first, after the value the write had set when it had landed, so that normally nothing is left (`result=refused`, `created=0`, with the reason it stopped for: `key_is_link`, `concurrent_change` or the Win32 token; after an exception the plugin's fixed failed audit line, caveat 2). The rule is the same without an attacker: a create that fails part-way under a plain parent (say `access_denied` on the second component) also removes the first. A key a create merely opened is closed, never deleted. The rollback is BEST EFFORT. A key that holds a value or a subkey when the rollback checks it is kept, because `NtDeleteKey` would destroy the values with it (the rollback asks `RegEnumValueW` first), and so is a key whose delete failed: each is counted in the audit line (`result=failed`, `created=<n>`). Windows has no delete-if-empty call, so two windows stay open: a value another writer puts into the key between that check and the delete is deleted with the key, and a value another writer puts over our own same-named value before the rollback deletes it by name is deleted with it. After a double fault (a rollback step that itself fails or throws) the value and the keys can stay with `created=-` and nothing logged. One derivation serves every hive, `HKCU` and `HKCR` included, and costs two `final_name` calls per walk whatever the depth. It is always used for `HKCU` (it resolves per calling user) and `HKCR` (a merged view of two trees), neither of which has one kernel name to compare with, for a key that is missing, and whenever the fast open declines. It alone produces the verdict token and creates: a missing component is created component-wise from the checked parent, a create that finds the key already there refuses `concurrent_change`, and a creating action never creates a key directly beneath the hive root (`root_level_create`).

The two differ in exactly two ancestor-only cases where the walk is the stricter (see Caveats); in both the write lands on the real requested key, as registry 1.0.0's single open did. A path under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet`, itself a link to the active control set, is refused on both: write under `HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001` (or the numbered set `Select\Current` names); registry 1.0.0 followed it, reads still do. `set_value` writes any of the six types (`REG_SZ`, `REG_EXPAND_SZ`, `REG_BINARY`, `REG_DWORD`, `REG_MULTI_SZ`, `REG_QWORD`) from text or exact `data_hex` bytes, reads the value back on the same handle and compares type and bytes; a mismatch fails the action (`verify_mismatch`). `delete_key` refuses a key that has subkeys (`key_has_subkeys`) unless `recursive=true`, and deletes by handle with `NtDeleteKey`, never `RegDeleteTreeW`, which follows a registry link met inside a tree; a link at the leaf is opened as the link object, so the delete removes the link and never its target. Without `recursive` its counts are what the key held: `counted_keys|1` and `counted_values|<n>`, with `capped|1` when the value enumeration stopped at its cap of 10,000 nodes, the key plus up to 9,999 values (`counted_values` is then a lower bound; the delete still removes the key with all its values). Every mutating action captures the previous value first and emits ONE `audit|` line per operation (see "Audit line grammar and producer contract"; `apply` emits one per plan item it attempts).

**Recursive `delete_key`.** `recursive=true` first VETS the tree (`count_tree`): every child is opened from its parent's handle with `REG_OPTION_OPEN_LINK` and the delete's own access (`DELETE` included, so a child whose ACL denies the delete refuses the call before anything is removed) and probed for `SymbolicLinkValue`, up to 10,000 keys and values and 600 levels (one open handle per level is held, at most 601); a security product that lets the open through and refuses only the delete itself is invisible to the vet and stops a real run part-way. A link anywhere in the tree refuses the call `key_is_link` with nothing deleted, and so does a child whose raw UTF-16 name is not well-formed (a lone surrogate or a NUL: its lossy U+FFFD spelling would open a sibling, or nothing), as `unrepresentable_name`; a tree the vet could not finish is refused `tree_too_large` when the delete is real (a dry run reports the lower bound with `capped|1`). `dry_run=true` stops there: `status|ok`, the vet's counts, `dry_run|1`, nothing deleted. The real delete (`delete_subtree`) is post-order: every child it finds AT DELETE TIME is opened again with `DELETE` and probed again, and removed by `NtDeleteKey` on its own handle; a removed child no longer enumerates, so the loop asks for index 0 until none is left. **The vet is a size bound and a link sweep, not a list of the keys it saw.** A key added under the tree after the vet is deleted and counted like any other (it sits under the key the operator named); a link added since is refused `key_is_link`, and a child with a malformed raw name added since `unrepresentable_name` (the keys already removed stay counted and the result is `failed`); a tree that outgrew the bound stops `concurrent_change`. The counts of a real run are what was REMOVED (exact when it succeeds, the partial total when it stopped), so they can exceed a dry run's snapshot. A link key whose `SymbolicLinkValue` lands after its probe is still only ever deleted as the link object by its own handle and has no children to enumerate; the walk does not repeat the kernel-name check per child (one `NtQueryKey` each, on the delete path): it relies on a link key enumerating no children.

**Per-user writes (`set_user_value`, `delete_user_value`).** The profile is resolved as `get_user_value` resolves it (`resolve_profile`), and the core's `set_value_verified` / `delete_value_verified` then run on the ROOT of the hive `with_user_hive` hands over: the live `HKEY_USERS\<SID>` hive when the user is logged in (no lock), otherwise the offline `NTUSER.DAT` mount, under the process-wide `offline_hive_mutex` for the whole arm and behind the DEFAULT-ON hive-file guard (no custom check, so no deadline; it refuses, among others, an `NTUSER.DAT` with a second hard link, `hive_hardlinked`, so a write cannot be redirected into another hive file). The root of a user hive has no kernel name the fast open could compare, so a per-user write takes the walk, which never creates a key directly beneath the hive root (`root_level_create`). On the offline arm the written key is flushed with `RegFlushKey` before the unload (`flush_on`), because `RegUnLoadKeyW` does not itself modify the file; a flush that fails fails the write (`flush_failed:<token>`: durability is unknown; a creating write's keys are rolled back, an overwrite keeps its verified value in the mounted hive). After the unload the plugin probes `HKU\<SID>` once (`classify_offline_write_race`): a hive that has become LOADED means a session loaded the file after the write returned and is reported as `warning|hive_loaded_after_offline_write`; a logon that failed while the hive was mounted leaves no trace (caveat 4). `render_user_write` orders the output: the `hive_unload_failed` warning first, then the terminal hive error naming the guard's token, then the race warning, then the audit line (`hive=HKU`, `sid=<SID>`; a hive that was not reached or was refused is `result=refused` with `hive_not_found`, `privilege_missing`, `hive_mount_failed` or the guard's token as the reason; a durable write whose mount then failed to unload stays `result=ok` with `reason=hive_unload_failed`) and `status|ok` / `error|<token>`.

**`apply`.** One `plan` (a JSON array of at most 256 flat objects, at most 64 KiB) of `set_value`, `delete_value`, `create_key` and non-recursive `delete_key` items on `HKLM`, `dry_run` true by default. `parse_plan` refuses a whole plan on a shape error (`invalid_plan:<why>[:<index>]`) or as `dependent_items:<i>:<j>` (two value ops on one key and name, or a key op over another item's equal, ancestor or descendant key, ASCII-case-insensitively; two value ops on one key are also dependent whenever either name holds a non-ASCII character, because Windows folds value-name case with a Unicode table the parser cannot reproduce), so no item's verdict depends on an earlier one and a dry run can equal a real run; every other defect rides its item (`invalid_hive`, a bad path or name, a value that does not encode). `run_apply` opens each DISTINCT key that exists or is created once, on a checked handle (the first item on it does the open; `HKLM` is fast-eligible), and every later value item on that key reuses the handle; a FAILED open is never cached, so each item on a missing or refused key opens it again, and a `delete_value` on a missing key followed by a `set_value` on it still creates the key. Per item it captures the facts, takes the ONE verdict function (`refusal_reason`), identically in both modes, and only a real run then mutates and verifies; its verdicts are `would_apply` / `applied` / `refused` / `failed` / `skipped`. The dry run opens with the mutation's own access mask and, where a real run would create, asks for create access on the deepest existing key by a self re-open with `KEY_CREATE_SUB_KEY` (nothing is created); a first component missing under the hive root is `root_level_create` in both modes. **That probe has a limit, stated plainly: it proves create access on the existing parent, not the ACL a key that does not exist yet will inherit.** A real run can therefore still be refused or fail where the dry run said `would_apply` (the keys it made are rolled back by handle and `created` reports any that stayed). `delete_key` in a plan is non-recursive and refuses a link leaf (no op recreates a link); it vets EVERY value of the leaf by streaming (`vet_leaf_values`: up to the 10,000-node bound, past which the item is `tree_too_large`) and refuses `unsupported_old_type` or `unrepresentable_name` before deleting. The plan is NOT transactional: `continue_on_error=false` stops at the first refused or failed item and reports the rest `skipped`; the exit code is 1 and `error|partial_failure` closes the reply whenever any item was refused or failed. Every key path and value name a manifest row carries must read back exactly (`representable`, "The exact-name rule" under Outputs), and one 512 KiB budget bounds the undo manifest. Nothing is persisted on the endpoint: the undo manifest is the reply, and how to read and replay it is under Outputs.

Code anchors (file and function; line numbers move with every edit): the fast open `open_fast`, the checked walk `open_checked`, its name test `leaf_name_check` and its link probe `probe_link`, the guarded value read `query_value_bounded`, the verifying write `write_value_on`, the by-handle delete `delete_key_on`, the recursion `count_tree` / `delete_subtree` and the counts in `delete_key_tree`, the flush `flush_on`, the per-user output `render_user_write`, the apply layer `refusal_reason` / `vet_leaf_values` / `run_apply` (all in `registry_core.hpp`); the plan and row layer `parse_plan`, `representable` and `row_field` (`registry_plan.hpp`); the encoders `encode_value`, `validate_key_path`, `render_audit_line`, `restorable` and `classify_offline_write_race` (`registry_parsers.hpp`); the kernel calls `Win32Registry::open_path`, `final_name`, `root_name`, `delete_key_by_handle` and `flush_key` (`registry_win.cpp`); the server-side binding `registry_audit_events_for_frame` (`server/core/src/plugin_result_audit.hpp`).

inputs.description: A JSON array of up to 256 flat objects (64 KiB at most). Fields (all strings): `op` (set_value, delete_value, create_key or delete_key), `hive` (HKLM, the default and the only one), `key`, `name`, `type`, `value`, `data_hex`. set_value takes type (default REG_SZ) and value or data_hex, exactly as the set_value action; a present but empty `data_hex` is the zero-byte form (REG_BINARY only), which lets a captured empty value round-trip. delete_value takes key and name; create_key and delete_key take key only (delete_key is NOT recursive and refuses a link). A set_value or create_key item whose first key component does not already exist directly under the hive is refused root_level_create, in a dry run and a real run alike. An agent still on registry 1.x or 2.0.x answers `error|unknown action`.
inputs.name: plan

inputs.description: "true" (the default) reports every item's verdict and changes nothing; "false" applies the plan. Any other spelling is refused as invalid_data (the direct command route, which has no enum, also accepts 1 and 0).
inputs.name: dry_run

inputs.description: "true" keeps applying later items after a refused or failed one; "false" (the default) stops and reports the remaining items skipped.
inputs.name: continue_on_error

inputs.description: "true" deletes every subkey and value beneath the key as well; "false" (the default) refuses a key that has subkeys. The tree is vetted first (at most 10,000 keys and values and 600 levels, else tree_too_large with nothing deleted; a registry link inside it is refused as key_is_link), and the counts of a dry run are a snapshot. Any other spelling is refused as invalid_data (the direct command route, which has no enum, also accepts 1 and 0). Needs registry 2.1.0 on the agent: registry 1.x and 2.0.x ignore it.

inputs.description: "true" counts what a real run would remove (with `recursive`, the vetted tree) and deletes nothing; "false" (the default) deletes. Any other spelling is refused as invalid_data (the direct command route also accepts 1 and 0). Needs registry 2.1.0 on the agent: an agent at registry 1.x or 2.0.x ignores this flag and DELETES a key that has no subkeys, so upgrade agents first (docs/user-manual/upgrading.md).

inputs.name: name

inputs.description: The value data to write, as text; interpreted per `type`: decimal digits for REG_DWORD / REG_QWORD, literal text for REG_SZ / REG_EXPAND_SZ, LF-separated non-empty records for REG_MULTI_SZ (split on LF only, so a CR stays inside its record; an empty record or a trailing LF is refused as invalid_data; empty text is the empty list), hex digits for REG_BINARY (empty is zero bytes). Send exactly one of `value` and `data_hex`. When neither is sent, or the one sent is empty, the write stores an empty value of the type and answers ok: an empty string, the empty list or zero bytes (REG_DWORD and REG_QWORD refuse it as invalid_data), so a misspelt parameter name writes an empty value instead of failing. Through MCP `execute_instruction` and the result-set execute routes every parameter value is limited to 64 KiB.
inputs.name: value

inputs.description: The exact bytes to write, as hex, for any type; give it INSTEAD of `value` (both non-empty is refused as invalid_data). Shape is checked per type: 4 bytes for REG_DWORD, 8 for REG_QWORD, a terminating NUL for the string types, a trailing double NUL for REG_MULTI_SZ. Use it for exact bytes you hold from another source. An empty `data_hex` is the same as omitting it here. The plugin takes at most 1 MiB of data (2,097,152 hex characters), but MCP `execute_instruction` and the result-set execute routes limit every parameter value to 64 KiB, so through them it carries at most 32 KiB of data; the direct command route is not under that cap. Needs registry 2.0.0 on the agent: registry 1.x ignores it and writes an EMPTY REG_SZ over the value, answering `status|ok` (with type=REG_DWORD and data_hex only, 1.x throws and writes nothing).
inputs.name: data_hex

inputs.description: Registry value type to write. Defaults to REG_SZ when omitted. Mixed fleets: an agent still running registry 1.x stores REG_QWORD, REG_MULTI_SZ, REG_EXPAND_SZ and REG_BINARY values as REG_SZ text and answers `status|ok`, so upgrade the agents to registry 2.0.0 before using them.

columns.description: Row shape discriminator (field 0). Values: item, undo, audit, summary. A closing `error|partial_failure` line, which has no row_kind, follows the summary whenever any item was refused or failed.

columns.description: item and undo: the plan item index (0-based). audit: op=apply.<op>. summary: the item count.
columns.name: field_1

columns.description: item: the op (set_value, delete_value, create_key, delete_key). undo: the value name ("-" for the default value). audit: hive=. summary: items applied (or that would apply in a dry run).
columns.name: field_2

columns.description: item: the hive. undo: the value type. audit: result= (ok, refused, failed). summary: items refused.
columns.name: field_3

columns.description: item: the key path (exact for an item that proceeds). undo: the value data as hex (the kept bytes, then ~<total> when the capture was cut). audit: reason=. summary: items failed.
columns.name: field_4

columns.description: item: the value name ("-" for none or the default value; exact for an item that proceeds). undo: 1 when the capture was cut, else 0. audit: verify=. summary: items skipped after a stop.
columns.name: field_5

columns.description: item: the verdict (would_apply in a dry run, applied, refused, failed, skipped). audit: key= (capped at 256 bytes). summary: 1 for a dry run, 0 for a real run.
columns.name: field_6

columns.description: item: the refusal or failure token (key_not_found, value_not_found, key_has_subkeys, key_is_link, access_denied, root_level_create, tree_too_large, unsupported_old_type, unrepresentable_name, verify_mismatch, invalid_* ...) or "-". audit: name= (capped). summary: 1 when the undo manifest is complete, 0 when anything was cut or a creating item failed part-way.
columns.name: field_7

columns.description: item: the read-back verification (ok, mismatch, "-"). audit: type=.
columns.name: field_8

columns.description: item: the number of key components this item created (reverse: delete_key of each, deepest first), predicted in a dry run. audit: len=.
columns.name: field_9

columns.description: item: the previous value state (absent, present, unreadable) for value ops; "-" for a key op and for an item refused before its previous value was read (never read as absent). audit: dry_run=.
columns.name: field_10

columns.description: item: the previous value type. audit: counted_keys= ("-" for a delete_key that was invalid or whose open failed).
columns.name: field_11

columns.description: item: the previous value as hex (the kept bytes, then ~<total> when it was cut or the undo budget dropped it); restore it with data_hex. audit: counted_values=, or "-" when the item was refused before the contents of its key were read.
columns.name: field_12

columns.description: item: the new value length in bytes, or "-". audit: capped=, or "-" when not read. (The six audit tokens that follow -- created, sid, old_state, old_type, old, new -- are in the raw row and the registry.write audit row.)
columns.name: field_13

columns.description: Confirms the run succeeded and, on a real run, that the handle read back as deleted (a dry run answers ok too); only ever emitted on success — a failure is reported as an `error|<token>` line (not exhaustive: key_not_found, key_has_subkeys, tree_too_large, key_is_link, access_denied, verify_mismatch, concurrent_change, invalid_key_path, invalid_data or win32:<code>) and a non-zero exit instead of this column. A run that resolves its hive and key, success or not, also emits one `audit|op=delete_key|...` row (dry_run=1 on a dry run, whose success row records that a vet ran, not a deletion); a missing hive or key, or an unparseable hive, is a bare `error|...` line with nothing opened and no audit row. Values: ok.
columns.name: status

columns.description: Keys in the subtree, the target included: on a real run what the delete REMOVED (exact when it succeeds, the partial total when it stopped), on a dry run what the vet counted (a lower bound when capped is 1). A non-recursive delete counts the target alone, so 1. Emitted on success only: a refusal carries its counts in the audit row (counted_keys=). Values: a non-negative integer.
columns.name: counted_keys

outputs_note:
This plugin does not emit a uniform pipe-joined "row"; each action has its own shape. `get_value`, `get_user_value` and `key_exists` write one self-describing `field_name|value` line per field on success; a failure writes an `error|...` line and returns rc 1, so `-` is never used as an absence placeholder in the read actions. Every mutating action that resolves its target writes ONE `audit|...` line first (grammar below; `-` is "not applicable" inside it), then `status|ok` or `error|<token>`; a missing hive or key or an unparseable hive is a bare `error|...` line with nothing opened and no audit line, while a key path or value name that fails shape validation after the hive resolved is audited as `result=refused`; the dashboard shows the `audit` line as one more row. `delete_key` appends four `key|value` rows after `status|ok`: `counted_keys` and `counted_values` (without `recursive`, the key itself and the values it held; with it, the keys and values the delete REMOVED, or on a dry run the vet's count), `dry_run` (1 for a dry run, 0 for a real run) and `capped` (1 when the vet or the value count stopped at its bound, 10,000 keys and values and 600 levels, which makes the counts a lower bound; a real recursive delete past the bound is refused `tree_too_large` instead); the counts are point in time, since a writer racing the delete can add values the count never saw. `set_user_value` and `delete_user_value` write the hive lines first when there are any (a `warning|hive_unload_failed: ...`, the race warning, the terminal `error|...` of an unreachable or refused hive), then the audit line (`hive=HKU`, `sid=<SID>`) and `status|ok` or `error|<token>`. `apply` writes each item's rows as the item concludes, before the next item opens anything: its `audit|` line, its `item|` row and, for a `delete_key` that removed its key, one `undo|` row per retained value (an item skipped after a stop has only its `item|` row and no audit line); then one `summary|` row and, when any item was refused or failed, `error|partial_failure` with rc 1. A later exception inside the plugin, or a failed output channel, cannot take back rows already written; the agent sends output at command end or each 64 KiB, so an agent that dies mid-plan loses whatever it had not yet sent (for a plan under 64 KiB of output, all of it): read the keys back with a dry run before replaying anything. If the output channel itself fails after the first audit line, the plan stops there with `error|exception` (rc 1): nothing after that item is opened or changed, and no `summary|` row follows. A whole-plan refusal (`error|invalid_plan:<why>[:<index>]`, `error|dependent_items:<i>:<j>` or `error|invalid_data` for a flag that is not `true` or `false`, or `1` or `0` on the direct route) is a bare error line with nothing opened and no audit line. The row shapes (cells split on `|`):

| Row | Cells |
|---|---|
| `item` (14) | `item`, index, op, hive, key, name (`-` for none or the default value), verdict, reason (`-` when none), verify (`ok`, `mismatch`, `-`), created, old_state (`absent`, `present`, `unreadable`; `-` for a key op and for an item refused before its previous value was read), old_type, old_hex (the retained bytes, then `~<total>` when cut or dropped by the budget), new_len |
| `undo` (6) | `undo`, the index of the `delete_key` item, name (`-` for the default value), type, hex (the retained bytes, then `~<total>` when cut), truncated (1 when cut) |
| `summary` (8) | `summary`, total, applied (would apply, in a dry run), refused, failed, skipped, dry_run (1/0), undo_complete (1/0) |

The key and name cells of an item that proceeds are exact (`representable`); a refused item's cells are the folded display form (a trailing backslash shows as `_`). An item refused before its previous value or its key's contents were read (an invalid item, one whose open failed, a `delete_key` refused for subkeys, or one whose vet or enumeration failed) shows `-` in its old_* cells and, for a `delete_key`, in the audit line's counted_* fields: `-` means "not read", never `absent`. A refused real creating item removes the keys its open made before its row goes out: `refused` with `created` 0 when all were removed, `failed` with the number that stayed otherwise. An `audit|` row is the same 20-part line as for a single action, with `op=apply.<op>`. `enumerate_keys` writes one `subkey|<name>` line per subkey; a genuinely empty key emits zero lines with rc 0. `enumerate_values` writes one line per value shaped `value|<name>|<type>` -- the leading `value` is a fixed literal tag, not one of the two documented columns (`name`, `type`); see Caveats. `list_profiles` writes one true pipe-joined row per profile (`<sid>|<name>|<path>|<state>`, no discriminator prefix) and zero rows is a structural success.

**The exact-name rule.** Every key path and value name a manifest row carries must read back as exactly what is in the registry, so one predicate (`representable`) decides: `row_field(name) == name` -- no `|`, no control character (TAB aside), no DEL, C1 control, U+2028 or U+2029, no invalid UTF-8, no NUL, no trailing backslash (the server's column splitter reads `\|` as an escaped pipe) -- and not the literal `-` (a row spells the default value that way). A name that fails it is refused `unrepresentable_name` before anything is changed, for the plan's own names and for every value of a key an item would delete. That value name is the raw UTF-16 name the registry enumerates and must be well-formed: one holding a lone surrogate or a NUL has no exact UTF-8 spelling (a display read shows the surrogate as U+FFFD, which names a different value or none), so it is refused the same way, in the dry run and the real run alike; a value really named with U+FFFD is deleted and restored like any other. So is a value whose name this plugin could not write back with `set_value` (a TAB, which `representable` accepts, or another control byte): on a `delete_key` item the token means "the manifest could not restore it by that name". A previous value this plugin could not write back (`REG_NONE` or another type it cannot write, a shape it would refuse, over 1 MiB) is `unsupported_old_type`.

**The undo budget.** One 512 KiB `CaptureBudget` charges every retained byte (the data, the name and 64 bytes per row) BEFORE anything is kept; a row that does not fit is not retained and the summary says `undo_complete|0`, in the dry run too, so the operator sees an incomplete manifest before mutating. Each value keeps at most 4,096 bytes (a longer one is cut, which also makes `undo_complete|0`). The reply stays under the dispatcher's 2 MiB capture cap (`local_dispatcher.hpp`): the retained rows render to about 1 MiB of hex, at most 256 audit lines (each under 2 KiB) add 512 KiB, and the item rows and the summary about 100 KiB.

**Undoing a plan.** Save the dry run's and the real run's replies to the change record at once: the manifest exists nowhere else (the stored response is kept 90 days by default, `--response-retention-days`). Undo only the items whose verdict is `applied`, and those `failed` with `created` above 0 or with a mutation (a `failed` value write may have landed; a `failed` `delete_key` with `undo` rows took its values); `refused`, `would_apply` and `skipped` rows changed nothing. Replay in REVERSE item order. A row `name` of `-` is the default value: omit `name` in the replayed item (a plan refuses `-`). Per op:

| Op | What undoes it |
|---|---|
| `set_value` | the item row's previous value (`old_state`, `old_type`, `old_hex`): `present` -> `set_value` with `type` = `old_type` and `data_hex` = `old_hex`; `absent` -> `delete_value`; `created` above 0 means the write also made that many trailing key components -> `delete_key` of each, deepest first (one plan cannot hold a key and its descendant: `dependent_items`, so one call per level); `-` was not read and gives nothing to undo |
| `delete_value` | the previous value in the item row -> `set_value` with `type` = `old_type` and `data_hex` = `old_hex` |
| `create_key` | `created` above 0 -> `delete_key`, deepest first; 0 means the key existed and there is nothing to undo |
| `delete_key` | recreate the key from the item row (`create_key`; a key that held no values has no `undo` rows), then one `set_value` per `undo` row (name, type, hex) in a second plan (a key op and a value op on one key are `dependent_items`); a value whose name holds a non-ASCII character goes in a plan of its own when the key has other value rows (they would be `dependent_items`); a row cut or not retained makes `undo_complete|0` |

**What `undo_complete|1` means, and what it does not.** It means every previous value the plan needed was retained whole within the budget and no creating item stopped part-way leaving keys its `created` count cannot name. It speaks for VALUES only: a deleted key's owner, DACL and SACL, class and volatility are not captured, so a replayed `create_key` recreates it with the parent's inherited security, non-volatile and with no class (a key readable only by SYSTEM can become readable by whoever the parent grants; under a volatile parent the recreate fails). The manifest is a snapshot taken at capture: a value another writer changes or adds between the capture and the write or delete is lost, or stale, even with `undo_complete|1`. A reply that ended early (an exception, a dead agent, a failed output channel) has no `summary|` row and so no `undo_complete` at all.

**Error tokens of the mutating actions.** `error|<token>` and the audit line's `reason=` carry the bare token and nothing more, and the agent logs nothing about an ordinary failure (an exception is the exception: it is logged with the action name). What each means and where to look:

| Token | Meaning | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| `access_denied` | `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`, from several causes: the agent identity's ACL on the key refuses an access the action asks for (caveat 3 lists them); a parent the walk may traverse but not read (the walk opens every component with `KEY_QUERY_VALUE` to probe it; the fast open does not); a create refused on a parent, or an inherited ACL that gives the new key no `DELETE`; the link probe itself refused | the ACL of the key and of each parent for the agent identity |
| `key_not_found` | the key, or a component of the path, does not exist (nothing was written) | the spelling; `key_exists`; a `WOW6432Node` path |
| `value_not_found` | `delete_value` named a value the key does not hold (nothing deleted) | `enumerate_values` |
| `root_level_create` | the first key component is missing directly under the hive root; a creating write never creates one | the parent has to exist already |
| `key_is_link` | a component is a registry symbolic link, or the handle's kernel name is not the requested path (a link completed mid-walk, a component renamed, a non-ASCII case variant, a decoy value named `SymbolicLinkValue` on an ancestor); nothing was written, except in a real recursive delete that meets a link planted after its vet: the keys already removed stay removed, the counts say how many and the result is `failed` | the link's target path; the key's stored spelling |
| `key_has_subkeys` | `delete_key` without `recursive` on a key with subkeys (nothing deleted); an `apply` `delete_key` item on one | `recursive=true`, or delete the subkeys first |
| `tree_too_large` | a REAL recursive delete whose vet hit its bound (10,000 keys and values, 600 levels), or an `apply` `delete_key` item on a leaf with more values than that; nothing deleted | delete the tree in parts |
| `unsupported_old_type` | an `apply` item's previous value (or a value of a key it would delete) is a type this plugin cannot write (`REG_NONE`, `REG_LINK`, `REG_DWORD_BIG_ENDIAN`, unknown), a shape `set_value` would refuse, or over 1 MiB; refused before anything changed, so the change could not be undone | change it with another tool |
| `unrepresentable_name` | an `apply` key path or value name a manifest row cannot spell exactly (see "The exact-name rule"), a value of a key it would delete that this plugin could not write back by that name or whose raw UTF-16 name is not well-formed, or (a recursive `delete_key`) a key in the tree whose raw name is not well-formed | rename, or remove it with another tool |
| `flush_failed:<token>` | a per-user write verified, but `RegFlushKey` on the offline hive failed; durability is unknown | read the value back, retry |
| `hive_not_found`, `privilege_missing`, `hive_mount_failed`, a hive-file guard token (`hive_path_reparse_ancestor`, `hive_hardlinked`, ...) | a per-user write could not reach or trust the hive; nothing was written | the hive line above the audit line says why; for `hive_hardlinked`, find the second name with `fsutil hardlink list <path>`; a `hive_mount_failed` that persists for one profile can be a mount an earlier call failed to unload (`hive_unload_failed`, below) |
| `hive_unload_failed` | on a `result=ok` per-user row: the write is durable, but the offline hive stayed mounted | run the `reg unload HKU\<mount>` the warning line names once the process holding it lets go; until then the user's next logon can get a temporary profile |
| `concurrent_change` | another party created the key between the walk's check and its create, or the handle went stale (`ERROR_KEY_DELETED`), or a real recursive delete found the tree grown past its bound (the keys already removed stay removed, the counts say how many, `result=failed`) | read the key and retry; a recursive delete: dry run, then run again |
| `verify_mismatch` | the read-back differs from what was written, or the key did not read back as deleted. It can be a false positive: another writer, or a Group Policy refresh, that touches the value between the write and the read-back looks the same | `get_value` the value and decide |
| `invalid_key_path`, `invalid_value_name` | the input failed shape validation before anything was opened (limits under Inputs) | the parameter |
| `invalid_hive`, `dependent_items`, `invalid_plan:<why>` | `apply`: an item names a hive other than `HKLM`; two items touch the same value, two value items on one key carry a non-ASCII name, or items overlap on a key (the whole plan is refused `dependent_items:<i>:<j>`); the plan is refused whole as `invalid_plan:<why>[:<index>]`, `<why>` one of `plan_too_large` (over 64 KiB), `not_flat` (nested deeper than an array of objects), `not_json`, `not_array`, `empty`, `too_many_items` (over 256), `item_not_object`, `unknown_key`, `field_type` (a field that is not a string) or `invalid_op` | the plan; split dependent items into separate plans |
| `invalid_type` | `type` is not one of the six names (case-sensitive) | the spelling |
| `invalid_data` | the text or `data_hex` does not fit the type: not decimal digits for a number; not hex, or an odd count; a string without its terminating NUL; a REG_MULTI_SZ with an empty record or a trailing LF (records are split on LF only, so a CR stays in its record); `value` and `data_hex` both sent | the parameter |
| `value_overflow` | a number out of range for its type, or data over 1 MiB | the parameter |
| `win32:<code>` | any other Win32 or NT failure, by number, including the answer when `NtDeleteKey` refuses for a reason not listed here (caveat 4) | `net helpmsg <code>` |
| `exception` | an exception ended the action (an allocation failure is the realistic one); the audit line is the fixed failed line of caveat 2 (for `apply`, after the rows of the items already done; a failed output channel writes no fixed line) | the agent log, and "A partial or failed create" under Where the data goes; for `apply`, `error\|exception` after item rows with no `summary\|` row means the plan stopped there: trust the rows sent, compare a deleted key's `undo` rows with its audit `counted_values`, and read back the keys of the items with no row |

A misspelt or missing `value` parameter on a `REG_SZ`, `REG_EXPAND_SZ`, `REG_MULTI_SZ` or `REG_BINARY` write is not an error: it writes an empty value of the type and answers `status|ok` (`REG_DWORD` and `REG_QWORD` refuse it as `invalid_data`).

privileges.grant: Writes against `HKLM\*` need the service account in `Administrators`; `HKCU\*` needs no elevation. `get_user_value`, `set_user_value` and `delete_user_value` use the offline-hive fallback only when the target user is logged out: it needs `SeBackupPrivilege`+`SeRestorePrivilege`, already granted to the service account, so there is no new grant (the privileges are enabled on the PROCESS token for the span of the mount, a documented residual of `with_user_hive`); the live-hive path, the machine-hive writes (`apply` included) and `list_profiles` need no elevated privilege beyond the key's own ACL. `NtDeleteKey` and `NtQueryKey` (ntdll) need no privilege beyond `DELETE` on the key and a handle the caller already holds.
privileges.if_refused: `error|key not found` / `error|value not found` (reads; `get_value` answers `error|value changed while reading ...` for a value that kept growing through its bounded re-reads and `error|win32:<code>` for any other failed read); the mutating actions name the cause: `error|access_denied`, `key_not_found`, `value_not_found`, `key_is_link`, `key_has_subkeys`, `concurrent_change`, `root_level_create`, `verify_mismatch`, `invalid_key_path`, `invalid_value_name`, `invalid_type`, `invalid_data`, `value_overflow`, `tree_too_large`, `unsupported_old_type`, `unrepresentable_name`, `flush_failed:<token>`, `win32:<code>` or `exception`; the per-user writes add `hive_not_found`, `privilege_missing`, `hive_mount_failed`, a hive-file guard token (`hive_hardlinked`, ...) and `hive_unload_failed`, and `apply` adds `invalid_hive`, `dependent_items:<i>:<j>`, `invalid_plan:<why>` and `partial_failure` (the token table under Outputs says what each means)

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows/lines travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore (90 days), queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`.

**Audit log.** The server records a `registry.write` row only for a `registry` command whose agent-stamped `CommandResponse.action` is one of the six mutating actions; an agent older than this plugin stamps none and produces no rows. Principal, result, retention and the join to the operator's row: `docs/user-manual/audit-log.md`.

**Agent log.** The plugin's own `spdlog` error lines (for example `registry: <action> raised an exception`) carry no command id: the plugin ABI hands a plugin no command identifier. Attribute a command through the response and audit rows above, which are joined on the command id.

**A partial or failed create.** A `set_value` row with `result=failed` and `created=<n>` above 0, an `error|exception` reply, or an agent that stopped in the middle of a command can leave keys the call made (and, for a write that landed, its value). Take the hive, key and value name from the request that dispatched the command, not from the audit row: the exception row has `hive=-|key=-|created=-`, and the `command.dispatch` row carries only `registry:set_value -> N agent(s)`. The request parameters are in `executions.parameter_values` of the execution that holds the row's `command_id` (join on it; the command-to-execution mapping is reaped after 24 hours, so the join can come back empty, and then only the dispatching script, workflow or schedule holds the request), or in the dispatching script, workflow or schedule. A call creates only the trailing components of a path that did not exist and the leading ones existed before, and a pre-existing empty parent looks exactly like a created one; the rollback goes leaf first, so the keys a failed call leaves are normally the shallowest of the ones it made, but not when the leaf holds a value or key another party put there: the leaf is kept and every ancestor above it survives with it (`created=<n>` counts the survivors on a returning exit). Read the candidates with `key_exists`, `enumerate_values` and `enumerate_keys`, and decide per key: remove it with `delete_key` (it refuses a key with subkeys, so go leaf first, one call per key) only when this call's creation of it can be shown (for example an earlier `key_exists` for the path answered false) and it is empty; a key that holds a value you did not write is another party's and stays, and so does any key whose creation by this call you cannot show. For an exception whose audit line could not be written, and for an agent that died mid-command, there is no `registry.write` row: only the `command.dispatch` row and the stored response show the attempt. A recursive `delete_key` stopped that way can leave the tree partly deleted with no row at all (a large tree takes seconds): run it again as a dry run to see what is left, then for real. An `apply` stopped that way keeps the rows the agent had already sent; an item with no row may still have run (the agent sends output in frames of up to 64 KiB), so read the keys of those items back before replaying anything. An `apply` that answered `error|exception` after item rows, with no `summary|` row, stopped there: its rows stand, a deleted key's manifest is whole only when its `undo` rows number its audit `counted_values`, and the keys of the items with no row are read back before replaying anything.

**Not consumed by** daily-sync inventory, the TAR warehouse, DEX, or metrics: nothing here runs on a schedule; the plugin executes only when an operator or workflow dispatches one of its twelve definitions.

**Sensitivity.** The audit rows of every mutating action (`apply` and the per-user writes included) and the `set_value`/`delete_value`/`set_user_value`/`delete_user_value` responses carry registry data OLD and NEW (hex of the raw bytes, 256 bytes at most per value in an audit row, for every value type) and key paths; an `apply` reply also carries its undo manifest, the previous value of each value item and every value of each deleted key (up to 4,096 bytes per value and 512 KiB per reply), readable by `Response:Read` holders for 90 days. All of these can hold secrets that live in the registry (a service account's autologon password, a product key, an agent token). **Owner risk acceptance:** old and new values are recorded as raw hex and can contain secrets; the product owner accepted this risk on 2026-10-20 and masking is a planned later change, and nothing in the plugin redacts them today. A key path can name a person. `get_value`/`enumerate_values`/`get_user_value` can return arbitrary registry data, among it `RegisteredOwner`/`DigitalProductId` (a person's name and a device-specific product-key hash); `get_user_value`'s `username` and `list_profiles`' `profile_name`/`profile_path` (e.g. `jsmith`/`C:\Users\jsmith`) directly identify a person and their home directory. The readers are wider than the writers: `AuditLog:Read` and `Response:Read` (the Viewer, Operator, PlatformEngineer, ITServiceOwner and Administrator roles hold both; `Response:Read` is not floored while RBAC is off), the legacy `/events` stream (any authenticated non-service-scoped session) and MCP `query_audit_log`; the executions' `parameter_values` carries the write parameters unredacted: `value` and `data_hex` of `set_value` and `set_user_value`, and the whole `apply` `plan` with every value in it. By default audit rows are retained 365 days (`--audit-retention-days`) and the response store 90 days (`--response-retention-days`); the executions table is not in the server's retention settings and no pass prunes it, so `parameter_values` stays until the database is purged. Read-time redaction is not built.
**Siblings:** none. Guardian's own real-time registry-key watch (`guard_type: "registry"`) is an unrelated detection mechanism; this plugin is on-demand only, with no watch/trigger surface.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary) -> `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) -> `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("windows.registry.get_value")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`; the audit rows: the audit log API filtered on `registry.write`.
